yes. Sorry for my vague question.
I am trying to use a JS model as a Multi-state model (Chapter 10.3.2 from Kery, 2011)
Using the book as a template I can build the following states:

4 hidden states. "not yet enter", "young", "Adult", "Dead".
and 3 observed states: "not seen", "Seen as young", "seen as an adult".

The model can be drawn in the following way:

>From here, I am able to build the transition matrix for the hidden part and the observation process.

The entry probabilities follow a Dirichlet distribution, to ensure that they will sum up to 1.
The transition probability from Y to A, depends on an individual covariate F
While the transition prob from A to D depends on F and the Age

The simulation that I use just considers the age and the individual covariate F to affect survival.
I am trying to see if the model can capture this effect, by studying the parameters \alpha_1 and \alpha_2.

So far I have not found any luck. I study 4 different simulated populations:
\alpha_1 and \alpha_2 different from 0
\alpha_2 = 0
\alpha_1 =0
\alpha_1 =0 and \alpha_2 =0
In all the scenarios convergence of the model is obtained. the posterior distributions for the population size and observation probability seem to be constant.
The posterior distribution of \alpha_1 is close to zero (and has 0 in the 95%CI), even when there is no effect (Scenario 3)
The posterior distribution of \alpha_2 has an effect on age, even where it should be zero (Scenario 2)

One final comment:
The model works with Data Augmentation. The augmented data of my observation process and the hidden process are 1 (not seen) for the observed process.
For the individual covariates and age, the augmented values are sampled from seen observations.

I would like to know if there may be a fault with my idea, or just the model is not made to find such effect.

Thank you for your help and time reading :)

--

Kéry, M., & Schaub, M. (2011). Bayesian population analysis using WinBUGS: a hierarchical perspective. Academic Press.

I am using repeat-transect electrofishing data and it is likely that the individuals captured do not occur independently of each other nor randomly.

Jacqueline

Hi Jacqui, Frederik,

personally I like the Poisson-lognormal (PLN) better than the NegBin, because I understand it better. But in terms of the inferences they are typically pretty similar. If you want to fit the NegBin in JAGS, you will want a re-parameterization in terms of the mean. We have BUGS code for this in Section 7.6 (pages 336-337) in the AHM1 book and if you don't have access to that, then you should be able to find that code on the book website.

Just beware of unreasonably high abundance estimates under the NegBin (and presumably also the PLN), which may sometimes arise.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear all, this post is quite old but I'm running into similar issues of unequal time intervals in a CJS model. I attached a chunk of my model, modified from Kery and Schaub. I'm trying to take daily survivals and extrapolate them into monthly (or pre-weaning, to be exact) survivals. However, I get gigantic credibility intervals and I wonder if the unequal sampling might explain this large uncertainty around survival estimates. I understand the concept of dummy 0's (ref Sanz-Aguilar et al. 2019), but how does it affect survival estimates exactly?
I'm also trying to avoid the Delta method, which I don't understand, and instead derive all survival estimates and their variance, but this might be for another post since I'm not sure I'm doing it correctly. That might be causing the giant CRI too.

My model is written in Nimble. I have no experience in using public list so apologies if this is useless or not understandable.

Le vendredi 23 décembre 2016 à 08:07:40 UTC-5, marc.kery a écrit :
> Dear Michael,
>
> thanks for confirming. So: the "least-cost" solution to unequal sampling intervals in CJS, MS and related models is then to fill in dummy occasions filled with all NA's and no other thing needs to be done, right ?
>
> Best regards --- Marc
>
> ________________________________________
> From: Schaub Michael
> Sent: 23 December 2016 13:48
>
>
> To: Kery Marc; Chloé Nater; hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> Subject: AW: Missing sampling occasions in CMR models
>
> Dear Marc,
>
> Yes, you are right - I haven't read this carefully enough - my answer refers to the case when there are 0 (not NA).
>
> Best wishes
>
> Michael
> ________________________________________
> Von: Kery Marc
> Gesendet: Freitag, 23. Dezember 2016 13:32
> An: Schaub Michael; Chloé Nater; hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> Betreff: RE: Missing sampling occasions in CMR models
>
> Dear Michael,
>
> but if all entries in the data are NA for an occasion, then I think you don't need to do anything else. p is simply not estimable and the posterior draws will be from the prior and you ignore them. I would think that you don't even need to fix the associated p's at zero or do anything else.
>
> Best regards --- Marc
>
> ________________________________________
> From: Schaub Michael
> Sent: 23 December 2016 13:25
> To: Kery Marc; Chloé Nater; hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> Subject: AW: Missing sampling occasions in CMR models
>
> Dear Marc,
> I think this is already the case. But then you have to tell the model that the p at specific occasions are 0, and that is what the sketched cosed is doing. An alternative would be actually to take these occasions out from the data set, and then no p Needs to be fixed. But then one has to deal with the unequal capture intervals when modeling survival.
> Best wishes
> Michael
> ________________________________________

> Betreff: RE: Missing sampling occasions in CMR models
>
> Dear Michael,
>
> wouldn't the easiest be to simply fill in dummy occasions with only NA's ?
>
> Best regards --- Marc

> To: Chloé Nater; hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> Subject: AW: Missing sampling occasions in CMR models
>
> The easiest way may be to apply a linear model on the recapture probability. You can create a vector X in such a way that the occasion without capture effort gets the same number (e.g. 40). Thus:
>
> X = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 40, 40, 40, 6, 7, ...]
>
> The model for p then gets something like:
>
> P[t] <- beta[X[t]]
>
> Priors:
> Beta[40] <- 0
> Beta[1...39] ~ dunif(0, 1)
>
> Best wishes
>
> Michael
>
> Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com [mailto:hmec...@googlegroups.com] Im Auftrag von Chloé Nater

>
> (I am aware that I could break the loops for p[t] up to manually define the affected p's as 0, but I am sure there is a more practical solution).
> Thanks alot for any help!
>

Dear Jacquie,

yes, there are many approaches to model selection and no agreement among statisticians about which is best.
You may not do model selection at all, but just build a single big model that has all potentially interesting terms in it and then present that. This isn't even as shocking as it may sound as first; for instance Gelman seems to have liked this approach for a long time.
Sequentially removing terms (= "backwards elimination") is an antique method that is still done since it's so easy.
Exploring variants of a single model ("iterating a single model") is something in between that has been advocated recently by ver Hoef, see   https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.891
Hooten and Hobbs (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0661.1) advocate model selection based on the predictive ability of a model. You can assess that in-sample (for the same data that you fit your model to) or out-of-sample (to new data). The latter is the gold standard, but more expensive (e.g., need more data)
Short-cuts are to estimate the predictive ability in-sample, e.g., as in AIC. Among the Bayesian counterparts of AIC, the WAIC seems to be the preferred information criterion recently. For instance, Jeff Doser's spOccupancy package gives the WAIC. You can code this up in JAGS for yourself, or alternatively use NIMBLE, which has a function to compute it for any (?) model
Cross-validation, including leave-one-out (LOO)-CV, is also a common method to assess the predictive ability of a model. An information criterion based on LOO is provided in Ken Kellner's ubms package. For models fit in Stan, there's the loo R package which allows computation of a LOO criterion from a single model fit. In principle, one can also apply that package with MCMC output from other software, but needs the log-predictive density of the data. This is not something that JAGS provides so if you wanted to stay with JAGS, you'd have to try to code that up yourself.
For Bayesian model selection in occupancy models, this is a relevant paper:  https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1
Best regards  --- Marc

Hi Marc,

Nice overview! Assuming that more people will find this useful, I’d just like to add RJMCMC to the list for variable selection. I have applied it for the inclusion of predictor variables, but also for the inclusion of random temporal effects (by toggling the sigma to 0 if it “shouldn’t” be included).

Cheers,

Matt

On Thu, 17 Feb 2022 at 20:16, Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

> Dear Jacquie,
>
> yes, there are many approaches to model selection and no agreement among statisticians about which is best.
> You may not do model selection at all, but just build a single big model that has all potentially interesting terms in it and then present that. This isn't even as shocking as it may sound as first; for instance Gelman seems to have liked this approach for a long time.
> Sequentially removing terms (= "backwards elimination") is an antique method that is still done since it's so easy.
> Exploring variants of a single model ("iterating a single model") is something in between that has been advocated recently by ver Hoef, see   https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.891
> Hooten and Hobbs (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0661.1) advocate model selection based on the predictive ability of a model. You can assess that in-sample (for the same data that you fit your model to) or out-of-sample (to new data). The latter is the gold standard, but more expensive (e.g., need more data)
> Short-cuts are to estimate the predictive ability in-sample, e.g., as in AIC. Among the Bayesian counterparts of AIC, the WAIC seems to be the preferred information criterion recently. For instance, Jeff Doser's spOccupancy package gives the WAIC. You can code this up in JAGS for yourself, or alternatively use NIMBLE, which has a function to compute it for any (?) model
> Cross-validation, including leave-one-out (LOO)-CV, is also a common method to assess the predictive ability of a model. An information criterion based on LOO is provided in Ken Kellner's ubms package. For models fit in Stan, there's the loo R package which allows computation of a LOO criterion from a single model fit. In principle, one can also apply that package with MCMC output from other software, but needs the log-predictive density of the data. This is not something that JAGS provides so if you wanted to stay with JAGS, you'd have to try to code that up yourself.
> For Bayesian model selection in occupancy models, this is a relevant paper:  https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1
> Best regards  --- Marc

Hello friends and colleagues,

First of all, apologies for cross-posting, and for hijacking this list, but I think it may be of interest to some of you and perhaps you can help share this.

We are very pleased to announce that we are now accepting applications for the third intake of our new MSc in Statistical Ecology. This 1-year MSc aims to give students

a sound understanding of the statistical foundations of modern methods in statistical ecology
knowledge and skills to use these methods effectively
experience of applying them to real-world problems, under the supervision of experts, some of whom are leading researchers in this field

The Programme involves two semesters of taught courses and a 3-month summer research dissertation. It is taught by staff at the interdisciplinary Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/). The summer dissertation includes optional placements with collaborators in the UK or abroad, to give students experience of dealing with real-world problems in statistical ecology.

We are delighted to announce that we intend to award scholarships to partially or fully cover MSc fees to selected successful applicants. This year we have the equivalent to 2 international / 4 home fee-waiver scholarships available, which can be applied for when applying for admission to the MSc.

More information is available here:

Course details: https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/subjects/statistics/statistical-ecology-msc/
Scholarship: https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/study/fees-and-funding/postgraduate/scholarships/statistical-ecology/
For any additional information, please direct enquiries to ma...@st-andrews.ac.uk.

Many thanks, and hope you are all keeping well.

Chris Sutherland

> On Thu, 17 Feb 2022 at 20:16, Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:
> > Dear Jacquie,
> >
> > yes, there are many approaches to model selection and no agreement among statisticians about which is best.
> > You may not do model selection at all, but just build a single big model that has all potentially interesting terms in it and then present that. This isn't even as shocking as it may sound as first; for instance Gelman seems to have liked this approach for a long time.
> > Sequentially removing terms (= "backwards elimination") is an antique method that is still done since it's so easy.
> > Exploring variants of a single model ("iterating a single model") is something in between that has been advocated recently by ver Hoef, see   https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.891
> > Hooten and Hobbs (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0661.1) advocate model selection based on the predictive ability of a model. You can assess that in-sample (for the same data that you fit your model to) or out-of-sample (to new data). The latter is the gold standard, but more expensive (e.g., need more data)
> > Short-cuts are to estimate the predictive ability in-sample, e.g., as in AIC. Among the Bayesian counterparts of AIC, the WAIC seems to be the preferred information criterion recently. For instance, Jeff Doser's spOccupancy package gives the WAIC. You can code this up in JAGS for yourself, or alternatively use NIMBLE, which has a function to compute it for any (?) model
> > Cross-validation, including leave-one-out (LOO)-CV, is also a common method to assess the predictive ability of a model. An information criterion based on LOO is provided in Ken Kellner's ubms package. For models fit in Stan, there's the loo R package which allows computation of a LOO criterion from a single model fit. In principle, one can also apply that package with MCMC output from other software, but needs the log-predictive density of the data. This is not something that JAGS provides so if you wanted to stay with JAGS, you'd have to try to code that up yourself.
> > For Bayesian model selection in occupancy models, this is a relevant paper:  https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1
> > Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi, everybody,

Fábio Wood and myself have been experimenting with alternative data formats in a multi-species, occupancy-dynamic model (similar to that in section 5.3.2 of AHM2). All is going well, but we realized that the output from JAGS analyses of vectorized and matrix-form data come out the same. That is, all estimates exactly the same to the seventh decimal place, which is the current limit of our numeric display.

Surprised, we tried to run the vectorized-format analysis several times and, again, the results from multiple runs come out exactly the same to the seventh decimal place. Our code does not have any sort of ’set.seed’ command.

Is this something weird that is happening to us alone, or does it happen to everybody else in normal circumstances? If it does happens to everybody else, what does it say about the random component of the MCMC algorithms implemented by JAGS? Should we not expect to get qualitatively similar but slightly different numerical results from different runs of the same analysis?

Thank you for any insight and my apologies if we are missing something obvious.

Gonçalo

Gonçalo Ferraz
Departamento de Ecologia, Instituto de Biociências
Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul
